title: Federal Judge Declines to Block Trump's New Birthright Citizenship Order but Questions Its Viability
excerpt: U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman rejected a temporary restraining order on procedural grounds but sharply questioned whether Trump's August executive order targeting birth tourism could survive legal challenge after the Supreme Court's sweeping June ruling.
body:
• U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman declined to immediately block Trump's August 6 executive order targeting birth tourism, ruling that the plaintiffs' lawsuit did not mention the new order
  • Boardman sharply questioned the order's viability, calling it "unprecedented" and noting the Supreme Court's June 30 ruling broadly rejected restrictions on birthright citizenship
  • The judge set a swift briefing schedule for plaintiffs to amend their complaint and mount a fresh challenge to the order
  • Federal agencies are expected to issue implementation guidance by September 5, setting the stage for the next legal confrontation

A federal judge on Friday declined to immediately block President Donald Trump's newest executive order limiting birthright citizenship, even as she sharply questioned whether the order could survive legal scrutiny following the Supreme Court's sweeping rejection of his previous attempt.

A Procedural Barrier, Not a Victory

U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Greenbelt, Maryland, rejected a request for a temporary restraining order sought by immigrant rights advocates. The groups, represented by the ACLU and other civil rights organizations, had previously secured a ruling from Boardman blocking Trump's initial 2025 executive order curtailing birthright citizenship.

However, Boardman said she could not block the new order because the plaintiffs' existing lawsuit did not even mention it. She allowed the groups to amend their complaint and set a swift briefing schedule to consider a fresh challenge, according to NDTV.

"As far as I can tell, this is unprecedented."

— U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman, on Trump's attempt to carve out exceptions to birthright citizenship

The ruling is a procedural setback for the plaintiffs rather than a substantive win for the administration. Boardman made clear her skepticism about the order's legal foundation, describing it as an attempt to "strike out exceptions to birthright citizenship with the stroke of a pen."

What's in the New Order

The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 on June 30 that Trump's original January 2025 executive order — which sought to deny citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants and temporary visa holders — violated the 14th Amendment's citizenship clause. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that the amendment's framers "extended that promise to 'every free-born person in this land.' We keep that promise today."

Undeterred, Trump signed two new executive orders on August 6 targeting narrower categories. The orders take particular aim at "birth tourism," in which women travel to the United States to give birth so their children can obtain citizenship. They also deny citizenship to children whose parents work for foreign governments, engage in fraud, or are classified as "alien enemies."

"That practice of birth tourism is, as of the signing of this order, hereby banned," White House aide Stephen Miller said at the signing ceremony, as reported by Reuters.

Legal Experts See an Uphill Battle

Legal scholars say the new orders face steep odds. The Supreme Court's June decision was broadly written, and experts argue it already addressed the categories Trump is now targeting.

"These children are citizens based on their birth on U.S. soil. Illegal conduct by their parent can have no bearing on their status."

— Amanda Frost, University of Virginia law professor

During Friday's hearing, Boardman pressed the administration on where the Supreme Court's ruling left room for birth tourism exceptions. Department of Justice attorneys opposed immediate action, noting federal agencies had not yet issued the necessary public guidance detailing how the directive would be implemented. That guidance is expected by September 5.

What It Means for Immigrant Communities

Birthright citizenship is a cornerstone of the American immigration system and holds particular significance for the Indian diaspora. Many Indian-origin families in the United States include members on various visa categories — H-1B, L-1, student visas — whose U.S.-born children are citizens under the 14th Amendment.

While Trump's latest orders focus on birth tourism and fraud rather than legal visa holders, the legal uncertainty has generated anxiety among immigrant communities watching constitutional boundaries shift. The ACLU's parallel challenge in New Hampshire and the Maryland proceedings set up a potential path back to the Supreme Court if lower courts diverge on the issue.

The next key date is September 5, when federal agencies are expected to detail how the birth tourism ban and related provisions would be enforced in practice.
